Council approved Bill #250568, authorising the sale of $800 million in bonds to pay for her Housing Opportunities Made Easy (H.O.M.E.) initiative, issued under a service agreement with the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority. The money subsidises the creation and preservation of 30,000 units built through public-private partnership rather than operated by the city, and her own framing is of streamlining processes and eliminating barriers so that housing gets built. That is subsidy and public financing to get affordable housing built, which is the chair 4 position, rather than chair 3's binding rules on the private market such as rent caps or required affordable units.

Parker signed Executive Order No. 7-25, her One Philly Plan to End Street Homelessness, during her State of the City speech on 19 December 2025. Its Section 1 is operative rather than advisory: it directs the Office of Homeless Services, in coordination with other City agencies, to facilitate access and provide financial support to operate 1,000 new shelter beds, to be operational by 31 January 2026, with on-site wrap-around behavioural health services and work with the Philadelphia Housing Authority on permanent supportive housing supply. Expanding the shelter system by 1,000 beds and directing financial support to operate them is chair 2, expanding services by increasing public funding. It is not chair 3, which is maintaining today's programmes with no major new spending, and it is not chair 1: the order sets a numbered expansion against a deadline rather than a permanent dedicated funding stream or a guarantee of housing.

Parker's first act in office was Executive Order No. 1-24, signed 2 January 2024, declaring a public safety emergency. It is not only a planning document: Section 2.A orders the Police Commissioner to employ any lawful means necessary to abate the emergency and the Department to vigorously enforce existing law, and Section 2.B sets the objective of increasing the number of police officers conducting patrol operations and maximising deployment of the current force. The Department's 100-Day Report, prepared in response to that order, records the delivery: strategies to maximise deployment of current staffing, strategies for increasing the number of officers trained for community policing, and 129 new officers assigned from academy classes to foot beats by the end of June 2024. Adding officers and expanding police presence to deter and respond to crime is chair 4. It is not chair 3, which keeps police as the main responders and adds crisis teams alongside them; the order's named objective is more officers and more patrol.

Parker signed six of the seven ICE Out bills into law on 7 May 2026, codifying Philadelphia's sanctuary policy in ordinance rather than leaving it to a predecessor's executive order. One of them adds Chapter 21-3600 to The Philadelphia Code, Non-Intervention with Respect to Immigration Enforcement. Its architecture is the judicial-warrant test: it defines an administrative warrant to include detainer requests while expressly excluding a judicial warrant or court order, and it bars City agencies from disclosing citizenship or immigration status unless required to do so by a judicial warrant or subpoena. The package likewise bars city agencies, including police, from collaborating with federal civil immigration enforcement absent a judicial warrant. Complying only on a court order is chair 2. Chair 1 is excluded by the document itself, which preserves 8 U.S.C. 1373 and states that nothing in the Chapter requires or permits violations of federal law, so local employees are not prohibited outright from sharing status information. It goes further than chair 3, which only declines proactive assistance: Philadelphia refuses the administrative detainer itself.

Johnson is the first-named sponsor of Bill 200593, enacted in December 2020, which amends Chapter 10-2000 of The Philadelphia Code to add prohibitions on using three-dimensional printers to make firearms and on the transfer, use or conversion of unfinished firearms and the equipment used to make them. Describing his own law, Johnson said it does not prohibit the manufacturing of guns but requires that it be done by licensed manufacturers in accordance with state and federal law. What the ordinance closes is the background check gap: the city's account records that the kits and individual pieces could be sold without the background check a buyer would face at a federally licensed dealer. That is chair 3 — every type of firearm stays lawful, and the route to one is made to run through licensed channels that carry a check. Chair 2 is excluded because the ordinance bans no class of weapon, which his own description states. Chair 4 is excluded because he wrote a new restriction rather than adding none.

Johnson is the first-named sponsor of Bill #250568, the ordinance authorising the service agreement and bond issue that finances the Housing Opportunities Made Easy plan. Council approved it unanimously, so the tally cannot carry a position and the evidence is his sponsorship. The instrument raises public money, a sale of 800 million dollars in bonds, and spends it on housing production and preservation, home affordability, home owner and renter assistance, contractor training, and blight and vacant property reduction. It places no binding rule on the private market: no rent cap, and no required share of affordable units. Subsidy at that scale with no mandate on private landlords or builders is chair 4. Chair 3 is excluded because the plan sets no such binding rules. Chair 2 is excluded because the city is financing production and preservation through a redevelopment authority rather than building and operating a public housing sector of its own.

Johnson voted for the eleven ordinances approving the 76 Place arena and the attribution is unusually clean: he chaired the Committee of the Whole, the report names the four members who voted no, and it states that all the other members in attendance voted yes. The margin, 12 to 4 in committee and 12 to 5 on final passage, is well past the 10 percent threshold, so the vote is usable. It still does not name a chair on this ladder. This ladder asks how much public money a government offers to attract a business, and this deal offered none. Two of the ordinances removed the site from a tax increment financing district and from a neighbourhood improvement district because the land would be city-owned and untaxed, and the developer paid the city rather than the reverse, with Johnson pressing it to raise its community benefits payment. Conditioning support on a larger community payment could be read as chair 3 or as chair 4, and nothing in the record decides between them, so the value is left blank.

Johnson voted for Bill 250044-A, which regulates security deposits between tenants and landlords. It passed 13 to 3, clearing the 10 percent rule, and the report names the three members who voted no, none of them Johnson, and records him congratulating the bill's sponsor on its passage, which places him in the chamber. The vote shows a direction favourable to tenants but it does not name a chair here, because every rung on this ladder turns on rent levels. Chair 2 would have him strengthening existing rent stabilisation and widening its coverage, and Philadelphia has no rent stabilisation to strengthen. Chair 3 would have him maintaining current tenant protections, which understates a vote that added one. A security deposit rule protects tenants while leaving rents untouched, so no rung describes it and the value is left blank.

Landau introduced Bill 250373-A, which amends Chapter 9-3500 of The Philadelphia Code, Fair Criminal Record Screening Standards, to amend definitions, add clarifications and enhance remedies. It passed 13-0, so the tally cannot carry a position and the evidence is her authorship. The law bars employers from screening applicants out on an old criminal record, and her amendment shortens the lookback period for misdemeanours from seven years to four, aligns city law with state law on minor summary offences, and holds employers to a transparent process. Her account of it is that the changes close loopholes, expand rights and add new enforcement mechanisms to strengthen the law's impact. Strengthening the enforcement of an anti-discrimination law, and widening who it protects, is chair 2. Chair 3 is excluded because she did not maintain the law as it stood: this is its sixth strengthening and she wrote it. Chair 1 is excluded because the ordinance governs how employers screen records rather than imposing equity requirements across institutions.

Landau wrote the Move-in Affordability Plan, the strongest tenant-side record on this council: one bill caps rental application fees at 20 dollars and the other, Bill 250044-A, lets renters pay a security deposit in up to four instalments. It passed 13-3, so the margin would have cleared the 10 percent rule. The value is still blank, because every rung on this ladder turns on rent levels and these bills do not touch rent. Chair 2 would have her strengthening existing rent stabilisation and widening its coverage, and Philadelphia has no rent stabilisation to strengthen. Chair 3 would have her maintaining the protections already in place, which understates an author who added two. A cap on move-in charges is a binding rule on landlords that leaves the rent itself to the market, and no rung on this ladder describes that.

Landau's record points at two chairs at once and does not settle between them. Her Move-in Affordability Plan sets binding rules on the private rental market, capping application fees and requiring landlords to accept a security deposit in instalments, which is the distinguishing feature of chair 3 and is flatly inconsistent with chair 4, whose whole claim is that no binding rules are set. But chair 3's examples are rent caps and required affordable units, which set the price or the supply of housing, and a cap on what a landlord may charge an applicant is a consumer protection rather than a rule about either. She has also backed public subsidy for housing production without writing a rule of that kind. The evidence establishes an interventionist direction and does not name a rung, so the value is left blank.

Gauthier is the first-named sponsor of Bill 210633-A, which amends Chapter 14-500 of The Philadelphia Code to create the Mixed Income Neighborhoods Overlay District. It passed 17-0 and was signed into law, so the tally cannot carry a position and the evidence is her authorship. The overlay requires that 20 percent of the units in any new housing development of ten or more units inside its boundaries be let or sold at restricted prices for 50 years, with at least three quarters of those units on site and a waiver route to the Housing Trust Fund for the rest. That is a binding rule on private developers requiring affordable units, which is chair 3 stated almost word for word. Chair 4 is excluded by the same fact, because its whole claim is that no binding rules are set and only subsidy is offered. Chairs 1 and 2 are excluded because the city builds and operates no housing under this ordinance; the obligation falls on the private builder.
